titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Ecuador to the Department of State

div.head: 396. Telegram From the Embassy in Ecuador to the Department of State
div.p: 10566. Subject: Secretary’s meeting with President-elect Rodrigo Borja.
1. Secret—Entire text.

2. Summary: President-elect Borja warmly welcomed the Secretary to Quito and expressed his hope for a close and productive relationship between our two countries. He stated that his administration would take a hard line against terrorism and narcotics, and that he welcomed continued mutual cooperation in these areas. Borja requested the Secretary’s assistance in avoiding a downgrading of Ecuador’s credit worthiness at forthcoming ICERC review, and asked for a 50 million dollar bridge loan to help the new government overcome a difficult foreign exchange crisis.

3. The Secretary expressed U.S. desire to continue the constructive relationship, and the willingness to reciprocate the Borja government’s approach toward that relationship. Regarding the 50 million dollar bridge loan, the Secretary noted that this is a decision for the Secretary of the Treasury, and approval would depend on having in place the necessary arrangements that would guarantee repayment of the loan. The Secretary noted that he would be making a public comment on the insult to the U.S. contained in the new mural at the Ecuadorian Congress, but that he would not allow the mural to deter him from attending the inauguration at the Congress. End summary.

4. The Secretary met with President-elect Rodrigo Borja for 50 minutes on August 10. Ecuadorian participants, in addition to the President-elect, were the incoming Minister of Foreign Relations Diego Cordovez, Minister of Government Andres Vallejo, Monetary Board President Abelardo Pachano, Central Bank Manager Jose Morillo, Secretary General for Administration Washington Herrera, the Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs Mario Aleman, and Ambassador Jose Antonio
Correa representing the Foreign Ministry’s Office of Protocol. The U.S. delegation included, in addition to the Secretary, Ambassador Holwill, Assistant Secretary Abrams, Assistant Secretary Redman, Deputy Assistant Secretary Gelbard, DCM Eisner (notetaker) and interpreter Van Reigersberg.

5. Borja initiated the conversation with a warm welcome to the Secretary and his presence at this democratic celebration of the people of Ecuador. He noted that those coming to the inauguration represented a wide spectrum of countries and ideologies, and their presence in Quito was reflective of the new Ecuadorian Government’s desire for pluralistic relations and its tolerance of diverse viewpoints. Borja continued that his government would seek the most cordial relations with the U.S. on the basis of a common democratic vocation and friendship. He looked forward to strengthening commercial ties, and to working out equitable solutions to conflicts in such key areas as foreign debt.

6. The Secretary expressed appreciation for Borja’s warm welcome, and delivered to the President-elect a letter from the President expressing good wishes for the new administration. He noted that his presence here as a special representative of the President was in support of freedom, the rule of law and democracy. These were the values that guided the U.S., and they were the basis of any just society. Differences of opinion would always exist between the U.S. and Ecuador. Mutual respect would be a key: The U.S. will frankly express its views with the intention of promoting common interest and working through differences. As friends, we are prepared also honestly to agree to disagree.

7. The Secretary noted the positive and mutual effort of the U.S. and Ecuador in the fight against narcotics and terrorism. These forces can tear a country apart, as we have seen in Peru and Colombia. The U.S., the Secretary said, is willing to continue to help Ecuador in these areas.

8. Referring to the area of economic cooperation, the Secretary stated that he looked forward to the opportunity to discuss over lunch these issues with
Borja’s economic team. He was interested in their views, noting that the decisions made in the first few weeks of an administration are often critical to eventual success or failure. It is easier to make tough decisions during an administration’s early honeymoon period, and then to enjoy the fruits of these policies three years or so down the road. The Secretary noted that it was a different age in which we lived—an age in which information was the key. Recalling a recent conversation in Rio de Janeiro, he noted that open and democratic societies were those best able to take advantage of this reality.

9. The Secretary noted that the U.S. is prepared to reciprocate the warmth and quality of the relationship that the Borja government wishes. The U.S. will respect Ecuador’s decisions. The message conveyed by the international media to the American people—by the presence in Quito of Daniel Ortega and Fidel Castro and by the new insulting mural on the walls of the Congress—was of a government turning sharply to the left. The Secretary noted that, in his own statements to the press, he was expressing that Ecuador is a friendly, democratic country that believes in the same values of freedom. His visit was an opportunity to pay respect to those shared values. The Secretary noted that he had been advised not to go to Congress because of the offensive mural. Despite the insult, he would go to the inauguration to underline U.S. support for Ecuador’s democratic transition. The
Secretary noted that he would have to make a statement to the press, however, regarding the insulting mural.

10. Borja stated that he had no doubt about the U.S. support for democratic regimes in Latin America. There were, however, three threats to democracy in the region. The Secretary had mentioned the first two—terrorism and drug trafficking. His administration would confront these threats with a strong hand, fully aware of the danger they pose to Latin American democracy. There was, however, a third danger not mentioned by the Secretary—the foreign debt. Borja stated that he had inherited a difficult domestic situation. He would need the U.S. comprehension and the Secretary’s personal help in working out a non-traditional approach that addresses the debt issue without destabilizing Ecuador and undercutting popular support for democracy.
11. Specifically, Borja stated that he had two requests to make of the Secretary:

list.item: Ecuador hoped for his support to avoid a down grading of the country’s credit worthiness at the forthcoming inter-agency country exposure review committee review. A “value impaired” determination would cause serious problems for the new administration in its effort to renegotiate its debt with the private banks.

Secondly, Borja noted that his administration needed a bridge loan of 50 million dollars. He was assuming office with negative foreign exchange reserves and with heavy food import needs. He stated that the problem, in part, was deliberately caused by the outgoing administration which wished to portray his government in the worse possible light by forcing a major devaluation of the local currency during his first weeks in office.

div.p:
12. Borja noted that his party, the Democratic Left (ID), was a moderate leftist and social democratic organization with ties to the socialist international. He, himself, was a Vice President of SI. The U.S. could be assured that, notwithstanding the negative image in some of the press, his administration would follow a moderate and democratic program. His administration had no intention of nationalizing any private firms because it knew that this was inefficient and lowered both the quality and quantity of production. Rather, his party’s roots were firmly planted in the same soil as those of Mario Soares of Portugal and Felipe Gonzalez of Spain. The party’s support came from the lower classes of Ecuador, and the Democratic Left Party was a bulwark against radical, communist
efforts to dominate the country.

13. The Secretary stated that Mario Soares and Felipe Gonzalez were very close and good friends. I am a pragmatic man, the Secretary continued, and, while I have my own philosophy, I have found that I can work best with those interested in solving common problems rather than indulging in dogmatic posturing. The Secretary noted that former Ambassador to Portugal Frank Carlucci had worked constructively with Mario Soares in benefit to both the U.S. and Portugal.

14. Borja expressed his pleasure in the Secretary’s having been “vaccinated” against the bad information on the Socialist International and its members. He noted that the continued existence of the ID was central to stability in Ecuador. The Secretary agreed and noted, looking around the room at the ID Ministers, that it looked to him that the party was in no danger of disappearing.

15. Recalling an earlier conversation with Felipe Gonzalez, the Secretary noted that the Spanish Prime
Minister had told him how he had learned from Mitterrand’s mistakes in France. Gonzalez avoided the pitfalls involved in trying to translate a strong electoral victory into sweeping socialistic reforms. Gonzalez had taken a pragmatic program, and Spain was now booming economically. Mitterrand had had the courage to admit his mistakes, and to reverse course before it was too late.

16. Borja expressed his amazement that there were so little differences in the way he and the Secretary saw the world. He had expected many more differences, but now concluded that the only distinction between the two was whether golf or tennis was the better game.

17. Turning to the discussion of foreign debt, the Secretary noted that there was general recognition that this was a serious international issue. It had been a central theme during his meetings in Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina and Bolivia had been the subject of general remarks that he had made in Montevideo. He would be pleased to provide to Borja’s economic team a copy of his remarks. The Secretary noted that, while countries would have to take tough measures, all the benefits of such reforms could not be restricted to creditors alone; incentives for Ecuadorians must also exist. At the same time, the Secretary stated the Borja regime is coming to power at a good time—the worse is over regarding the fall in oil prices and, hopefully, the nation would not suffer another damaging earthquake. Non-traditional exports were positive. With good economic management, Borja would be in a good position to argue for re-scheduling. Peru had started off by walking away from any solution to the debt problem and this had worked against a successful economic program. Working within the system, the Secretary stated that Borja should be in a good position to challenge the other members of the system to work with Ecuador in good faith.

18. Regarding the bridge loan, the Secretary noted that this was a matter within the competence of the Secretary of Treasury. As a former Secretary of the Treasury, he respected that Department’s preeminence in this area. The Secretary, however, stated that it would be helpful for Borja and his economic team to understand the concept behind a bridge loan. Fundamentally, it was a link between two piers, the latter pier an agreed and convincing program that guaranteed that the bridge loan would be repayed. As an example of a firm pier, the Secretary noted the recent Argentine agreement to undertake economic reforms that would release a pending World Bank loan. On the basis of this Argentine-IBRD understanding, the U.S. could offer a bridge loan to cover the period until the World Bank loan can be disbursed.

19. Borja expressed interest in the continuation of
the economic discussion during the Secretary’s lunch with his economic team. He hoped that the Secretary could discuss further the length of the bridge. The Secretary said he looked forward to the discussion, but that the focus should be on the strength of the press not on the bridge’s length.

20. Borja noted that he would like to mention the “small and big” problem of the mural at the Congress. He had only received information of the insult to the U.S. at a late date and had taken all efforts within his power to change the mural. He had had some qualitative changes made, but not all that was desired. It was hard to work with an internationally prominent and difficult artist. Borja stated that he very much appreciated the Secretary’s attendance at the inauguration, and expressed hope that the mural would not cast a shadow over the good relations he desired with the U.S.

21. The Secretary took his leave of the President-elect, again noting his intention to emphasize to the press that his presence in Ecuador was evidence of the good and warm relations the U.S. wanted with a fellow democracy. The meeting Ended.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880705–0074. Secret; Immediate; Exdis.

The letter has not been found. In telegram 9465 from Quito, July 20, the Embassy sent suggested letters from Reagan to Borja and Febres-Cordero. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880625–0651)
Shultz’s August 4 remarks to businessmen and bankers in Montevideo are in Department of State Bulletin, October 1988, pp. 8–12.
